scenes.narration: When you open your browser and type in your bank's website, or log into your email, or download a software update,

scenes.narration: The answer is Certificate Authorities, or CAs. Every browser and operating system on Earth comes pre-installed with a secret VIP list of root certificate authorities.
scenes.headline: Certificate Authorities
scenes.subline: Every browser ships with a pre-installed VIP list of roots.

scenes.narration: Those root CAs don't usually sign website certificates directly. Instead, they sign what are called Intermediate CAs, which are the workhorses that issue the digital passports, known as TLS certificates, to millions of websites.
scenes.headline: Roots sign intermediates. Intermediates sign websites.
scenes.subline: The digital passport is a TLS certificate.

scenes.narration: If you hold the private key to an intermediate CA, you don't just control one website. You hold a blank check for the entire internet.
scenes.headline: An intermediate key is a blank check for the internet
scenes.subline: Not one website. Any website.

scenes.narration: You can mint a cryptographically valid certificate for almost any domain on earth. Google, your bank, a software repository.
scenes.headline: A valid certificate for almost any domain
scenes.subline: The browser sees a trusted padlock. It has no reason to doubt it.

scenes.narration: And if that intermediate key is a code signing CA, you can stamp malicious Windows executables
scenes.headline: A code-signing key can stamp malware
scenes.subline: The executable inherits the CA's trust.

scenes.narration: so Microsoft Windows looks at your malware and says, yep, looks totally legitimate to me.

scenes.subline: The malware is signed by a CA the OS already trusts.

scenes.narration: Enter eMudra. Based in India and operating globally under the mSign brand, they are a massive trust service provider.
scenes.headline: eMudhra
scenes.subline: India-based. Global reach. The emSign brand.

scenes.narration: Their certificates are trusted by default in Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Apple Mac OS and iOS, and Microsoft Windows.
scenes.headline: Trusted by default on four platforms
scenes.subline: The root store is the front door.

scenes.narration: Even worse, they had eight of their intermediate certificates cross-signed by Sectigo, another giant certificate authority. That doubled the number of trusted certificate paths out in the wild to 16.
scenes.headline: Sectigo doubled the paths to 16
scenes.subline: Eight intermediates, two roots, sixteen trusted chains.

scenes.narration: and all eight of those intermediates used P384 elliptic curve cryptography.
scenes.headline: The curve was never the problem
scenes.subline: All eight used P-384. The private keys were one byte.

scenes.narration: Now, let's look at the math for just 30 seconds, because the contrast here is almost comical.
scenes.headline: Thirty seconds of math
scenes.subline: The contrast is almost comical.

scenes.narration: In P384 cryptography, your private key is supposed to be a randomly generated integer between 1 and roughly 2 to the power of 384.
scenes.headline: A P-384 private key is a random integer
scenes.subline: Anywhere from 1 to roughly 2^384.

meta.announce: A random integer with 384 bits of entropy.

scenes.narration: In normal decimal numbers, that is 115 digits long.
scenes.headline: A P-384 private key
scenes.subline: A random integer with 115 digits.

scenes.narration: In computer memory, it is 48 bytes of pure, unpredictable randomness.
scenes.headline: 48 bytes of pure randomness
scenes.subline: Every byte should be unpredictable.

meta.announce: 48 bytes of entropy. The key should be unguessable.

scenes.narration: Because elliptic curve math is a one-way street, everyone in the world is allowed to see your public key.
scenes.headline: A one-way street
scenes.subline: Everyone can see Q. Nobody can derive d.

scenes.narration: That public key is just a point on a mathematical curve, created by multiplying a known starting point by your secret private number.
scenes.headline: The public key is d times G
scenes.subline: A point on the curve, derived from the secret.

meta.announce: Q = d * G. Publish Q. Hide d.

scenes.narration: If your secret number is 115 digits long, reversing that multiplication is mathematically impossible.
scenes.headline: Reversing the multiplication is impossible
scenes.subline: That is the security proof for every P-384 key.

scenes.narration: But when eMudra generated eight of its intermediate keys, the first 47 bytes were all zeros. Every single one of them.
scenes.headline: The first 47 bytes were zeros
scenes.subline: The same pattern held for all eight keys.

meta.announce: 47 bytes of zero. The secret was the last byte.

scenes.narration: Only the very last byte at the end had anything in it. Instead of 2 to the power of 384 possibilities, there were only 255 possibilities.
scenes.headline: 2^384 possibilities became 255
scenes.subline: The last byte held the entire secret.
